attribution.note: Section heading in Zitron's own essay summarising his argument. The preceding paragraphs quote an engineer, but the heading is his own and he endorses it.

semantics.note: Keeps 'don't' plus 'never will' and the unreliability rationale. The present-tense part is folded into an unbounded firm forecast, which is a reasonable reading.

contract.note: Reading 'replace' as sustained, verified substitution for substantive engineering jobs, including avoided hiring, is an ordinary plain reading. It also fits the essay's focus on the engineering role. Treating the unreliability clause as a stated reason, not a condition, is fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic disclosure about itself, available before the evaluation date. Managers report hiring less because of AI, but this does not verify the scope of the substituted work or the remaining human work. The contract says an unsupported hiring claim does not meet the rule.
October 2026 S-1 describes autonomous work done alongside employees. It names no replaced engineering roles and gives no staffing counterfactual.

reviews.rationale: 'Never will' has no deadline, so no finite period can support it. The only way to settle it early is a corroborated deployment that verifiably replaces engineering jobs. The packet's evidence, Anthropic's hiring survey and its filing, are company disclosures without verified job scope or counterfactual. The early-resolution rule is not met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his essay.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim about capability plus a cost judgment. The drafter's version is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'the job' as reliably carrying a sustained engineering role under ordinary oversight matches the surrounding passage. Treating 'abominable' cost as an unscorable value judgment is fair. September 2025 is a reasonable window chosen by the evaluator.

evidence.note: In-period SWE-Bench Pro run: top models solve about 23% of well-specified repository tasks. This fits the 'fails' part, but it is a task benchmark, not a full-role evaluation, and it says nothing about cost.

reviews.rationale: The contract requires end-to-end evaluations of sustained engineering work and says task benchmark scores alone do not measure a job. The only evidence is a task benchmark with low resolve rates. That points toward the claim but does not meet the support condition. The cost part has no basis or comparator, so it cannot be scored. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. He paraphrases Brown for one clause but adopts it as his own.

semantics.note: Keeps the explicit 'because', the speaker's definition of software engineering, and the three stated limitations.

contract.note: Counting substantive repository maintenance and bug-fixing as engineering is an ordinary reading. The contract separates task success from owning a whole job and lets each component be judged separately. Whether 'can't do' means tasks or whole jobs still drives the result.

evidence.note: In-period tests on executable repository tasks: frontier agents solved about 23%. That contradicts categorical inability on substantive engineering tasks, though it does not show reliable whole-job performance.
Anthropic disclosure about August 2025, published December 2025. Employees fully delegate only 0–20% of their work and supervision matters. This supports the narrower limits on reliability.
A 2026 critique says SWE-Bench Pro scores may be inflated. This lowers confidence in e1 but gives no corrected figures.

reviews.rationale: The narrower limitations hold: low resolve rates, worse results on enterprise codebases, and limited full delegation all support poor reliability and the need for supervision. The categorical 'can't do software engineering' is contradicted under the contract by reproducible success on some repository tasks. The claimed causal mechanism (no learning or adaptation, degrading with more code) is not established.

attribution.note: Zitron's own rhetorical question, answered firmly ('No, not at all').

semantics.note: A firm present-tense claim about capability. The 'tension' clause is commentary and is rightly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'replace' as documented practical substitution for substantive acting or animation work is an ordinary reading. The 2025 year-to-publication window is evaluator-chosen but reasonable.

evidence.note: Trillo's 2024 Sora music video is outside the target period and does not document which acting or animation work was displaced.
OpenAI's February 2025 Critterz remake (mirrored) falls in the period, but it credits a human animator and does not show which work was substituted.

reviews.rationale: Neither item meets the contract. The 2024 video falls outside the period. The 2025 remake shows Sora being used in production but credits a human animator, without workflow detail separating substitution from assistance. No in-period evidence establishes that Sora replaced acting work or that it could not. The packet does not settle the claim.
